extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors querying literary agents / writers seeking traditional representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and a template for writing a one-page query letter to literary agents (primarily for novelists but with notes for nonfiction), explaining what agents look for and how to structure each section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query is a sales pitch / must be killer
rubrics_metrics.description: Your query is a sales pitch; no matter how terrific your manuscript is, without a strong query, no agent is going to bother setting eyes on page one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the query as a promotional email that must grab attention quickly. The blog emphasizes that queries 'suck' but are a necessary evil and that structure is intentionally formulaic to make the agent's job easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book must be finished (fiction) / strong proposal (nonfiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that is: Finished, if it’s fiction. (Nonfiction calls for a well-developed and convincing book proposal.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finished means written to The End; do not pitch a novel that isn't complete. For nonfiction, prepare a proposal including chapter summaries through the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable word count / length expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Finished also means that the word count is within an acceptable range. For mainstream adult fiction, that’s generally between about 70,000 and 100,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straying far outside these ranges (e.g., 50k or 150k) raises red flags: too short often means underdeveloped; too long suggests poor editing/filler. Check more detailed guidance where necessary and aim for typical ranges for your genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and subgenre fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Is in a genre they represent and a subgenre they regularly sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research agents' sales histories, Manuscript Wish Lists, interviews, and lists to ensure your book fits both genre and subgenre. Don’t waste an agent’s time by pitching a mismatched genre (e.g., romance to a thriller agent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fits an agent’s taste in tone and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Fits their taste in tone and style; sounds like books they already represent in tone or topic or style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show through your opening and query content that your book is similar in tone/topic/style to other books on the agent’s list—this is different from blindly naming genres; demonstrate specific tonal or stylistic affinities discovered via research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book should sound like a compelling read (compelling protagonist & clear arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using only the most essential details, make it clear that you have a compelling protagonist, and make his or her story arc clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the protagonist and stakes succinctly so the agent can picture the central conflict and arc. The goal is to entice the agent to request pages, not to retell every plot point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific — avoid vague themes and subjective claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific not generic. Avoid saying things like 'this is a story of love and loss' or using subjective claims like 'page-turning' or 'thought-provoking.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic thematic statements or empty praise tell the agent nothing. Instead, show why the story is unique by providing concrete details about characters, setting, and conflict. The post contrasts a thematic blurb with a character-focused, specific summary to illustrate the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize the opening to appeal to the agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalize your opening. Your first few lines are where you can immediately show them you’re querying them for a reason and that your book is right for their list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate knowledge of the agent (why you targeted them) without flattering them. Cite relevant sales, wishlist items, or interviews that show you researched their tastes. The opening should not be generic or clearly mass-sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence must grab attention and show intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents are unlikely to read past the first sentence, so the opening must quickly show that you’re querying them for a reason and introduce the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft an engaging, specific first line that signals genre/tone/fit; avoid dull or meandering openings. The blog stresses that agents skim slush piles and make quick decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a standard, professional format (don’t be original with structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of your query is not the place to be original! There’s a standard but effective formula you can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the tried-and-true template (sections 1–4 described below). Using conventional formatting makes the agent’s job easier and signals professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1 — Opening: agent personalization + title, word count, genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Section one should demonstrate that you’re a savvy professional pitching this particular literary agent for a reason. Next, quickly introduce your novel (title, word count, and genre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example intro: 'I’m hoping you will consider my 83,000-word historical novel, [Title].' Keep this simple and factual after your personalization sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 2 — Story summary: 1–2 paragraphs, specific, enticing
rubrics_metrics.description: Section two should tell the agent about the story and leave them wanting more. Summarize your book in one or maybe two paragraphs, enough to understand who and what the book is about but not a full plot rundown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to 'paint your book into a pretty little box that they can instantly understand BUT at the same time make it seem special.' Use the provided fill-in-the-blanks starter: 'MAIN CHARACTER, a ______________, desperately wants to _____________, but _____________ is getting in the way. To reach his/her goal, character tries _____________ but that plan fails because of _____________.' Add unique details about setting, stakes, and dangers. Avoid exhaustive CliffsNotes summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optionally include comparable titles (comp sales comps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optionally, you can compare your novel to other similar books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comps sparingly and thoughtfully—pick books that reflect tone, audience, or market position. This helps agents quickly understand where your book fits commercially, but it’s optional and should follow the story paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 — Author bio: relevant credentials and platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Section three of your query should introduce you and your background. If you have any writing credentials, this is the place to mention them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include publications, awards, MFA, prestigious conferences, residencies, or other relevant credentials. Also mention aspects of platform or ability to help publishers with publicity if applicable. If you have no publications, note other relevant achievements that demonstrate professionalism or audience reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4 — Closing: concise, polite, and follow submission instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: End with a short, polite closing (e.g., 'Thank you for your time and consideration'). If their submission instructions ask for additional materials like the synopsis or opening chapters, mention those attachments here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep closings brief and professional. Explicitly follow any agent-specific submission guidelines (attachments, sample pages, synopsis length, subject-line requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate professionalism and that you’ve done your homework
rubrics_metrics.description: You’ll show them that you’ve done your homework. You’ll be pitching something that’s like what they already represent or something new they’ve asked for. You’ll be polite. You’ll use a standard format to make their job easier. You’ll follow any submission guidelines they might have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalism includes accurate personalization, proper formatting, politeness, and strict adherence to an agent’s stated submission rules. This signals readiness to work with publishing professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the query concise — one page and not an entire synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing your entire novel in a one page query letter may feel impossible... the goal is not to give them a CliffsNotes rundown of the entire plot. It’s to get them to read more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit yourself to one page; the story summary should be brief and focused on essentials that motivate interest. Overlong, detailed synopses in the query itself are an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cut-and-paste mass queries and generic personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides cut-and-paste jobs blasted out indiscriminately... the second most common mistake is that authors focus on themes at the expense of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mass-send identical queries without tailoring. Generic flattery or obvious form letters reduce credibility. Personalization should be specific and evidence-based (cite a sale, wishlist, or interview).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction queries require proposal-level detail and chapter summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonfiction can be sold on proposal, but you still need to lay out a summary of each chapter through the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a convincing proposal with chapter-by-chapter summaries and market positioning rather than a short fiction-style query. Indicate how the proposal demonstrates completeness and marketability.
